section.title: Appointing Elders on Crete
section.sectionRationale: This is the reason Paul left Titus on Crete: to finish what was unfinished by appointing qualified elders in every town. Paul sets out the character of these leaders, then turns to the false teachers who must be silenced, quoting even a Cretan prophet against them. Leadership and the guarding of truth belong together in one movement.
section.thesis: Healthy churches need godly, blameless, doctrinally sound leaders who can both hold out the faithful word and stop the mouths of deceivers whose empty religion is exposed by their unfit lives.
section.frameNote: Two movements: the charge to appoint elders and the character required of an overseer; then the confrontation of the rebellious false teachers on Crete, whose profession is denied by their works.

verses.text: The reason I left you in Crete was that you would set in order what was unfinished and appoint {{presbyteros|elders}} in every town, as I directed you.
An elder must be {{anenkletos|blameless}}, the husband of but one wife, having children who are believers and who are not open to accusation of indiscretion or insubordination.
As God’s {{oikonomos|steward}}, an {{episkopos|overseer}} must be above reproach, not self-willed, not quick-tempered, not given to drunkenness, not violent, not greedy for money.
Instead, he must be hospitable, a lover of good, {{sophron|self-controlled}}, upright, holy, and disciplined.
He must hold firmly to the faithful word as it was taught, so that he can encourage others by {{hygiaino|sound}} teaching and refute those who contradict it.

units.label: Silence the false teachers
units.note: empty talk denied by their works

verses.text: For many are rebellious and full of empty talk and deception, especially those of the circumcision,
who must be silenced. For the sake of dishonorable gain, they undermine entire households and teach things they should not.
As one of their own prophets has said, “Cretans are always liars, evil beasts, lazy gluttons.”
This testimony is true. Therefore rebuke them sternly, so that they will be {{hygiaino|sound}} in the faith
and will pay no attention to Jewish myths or to the commands of men who have rejected the truth.
To the pure, all things are pure; but to the defiled and unbelieving, nothing is pure. Indeed, both their minds and their consciences are defiled.
They profess to know God, but by their actions they deny Him. They are detestable, disobedient, and unfit for any good deed.

presbyteros.gloss: An elder, a mature, appointed leader of the church. The term stresses spiritual maturity and standing. In verse 7 Paul uses overseer for the same office, showing that elder and overseer describe one role from two angles: seniority and responsibility. Every town was to have such tested men.

anenkletos.gloss: Blameless, above reproach, with no charge that can be made to stick. It does not mean sinless but of a settled, unimpeachable reputation. It heads the list of elder qualifications and is repeated in verse 7, framing the whole character portrait: a leader whose life gives critics nothing to grab.

oikonomos.gloss: A household manager or steward, entrusted with another's affairs and answerable to the master. The overseer manages God's household, the church, not as owner but as trustee. This frames leadership as stewardship: faithful care of what belongs to God, to be given back with an account.

episkopos.gloss: An overseer or guardian, one who watches over and cares for. Paul moves seamlessly from elder in verse 5 to overseer in verse 7, treating them as the same office. The word underlines the shepherd's watchful, protective duty toward the flock and the truth.

sophron.gloss: Self-controlled, sensible, of a sound and disciplined mind. It is a signature virtue of Titus, urged on elders, older men, young women, and young men alike. Against Crete's reputation for excess, this sober self-mastery is to mark God's people from top to bottom.

hygiaino.gloss: To be healthy or sound, the root of our word hygiene. Paul applies it to doctrine and to faith: teaching that is spiritually wholesome and health-giving, over against the diseased talk of the deceivers. Sound teaching in verse 9 makes for people who are sound in the faith in verse 13.

basic.context: Paul reminds Titus why he was left on Crete: to finish organising the churches by appointing elders in every town. He lists the kind of character these leaders must have, then describes the false teachers troubling the island, who must be silenced because their empty talk and greedy motives are wrecking households.
basic.hermeneutics: The list of qualifications is a pattern for choosing church leaders, focused far more on proven character than on talent or charisma. The sharp words about Cretans come from one of their own poets and are used to press the churches toward maturity, not to insult a whole people forever.
basic.originalLanguages: Paul uses two words for the one office: presbyteros, elder, and episkopos, overseer. The leader must be anenkletos, blameless, and an oikonomos, a steward of God's household. He must be sophron, self-controlled, a key Titus word, and able to give hygiaino, sound or healthy, teaching that keeps people sound in the faith.
basic.typology: The overseer as God's steward looks back to faithful stewards in Scripture and forward to Christ, the true and faithful Shepherd and Overseer of our souls. The godly elder is a small picture of the Chief Shepherd who cares perfectly for His flock.
basic.christ: Elders are undershepherds who point to Christ, the Chief Shepherd and Overseer of souls. They hold firmly to the faithful word, the gospel of Christ, and guard it against error. Their whole task exists to keep the church anchored to Jesus and His truth.
basic.god: God entrusts His household, the church, to stewards who must answer to Him. He cares that His people are led by those whose lives match their message, and He is not fooled by a profession of knowing Him that is contradicted by ungodly living.
basic.crossReferences: First Timothy 3 gives a parallel list of qualifications for overseers. First Peter 5 calls elders to shepherd God's flock under the Chief Shepherd. And Matthew 7 warns that a tree is known by its fruit, as these teachers are exposed by their works.
basic.oneStory: God has always gathered His people under shepherds, and He guards that flock by giving it faithful, godly leaders and by exposing false ones. Titus is to plant such leadership in Crete so the gospel takes deep root, part of God's larger work of building a people for Himself under the true Shepherd, Christ.

context.literary:
The body of the letter opens in verse 5 with a purpose clause that reaches back and forward at once. Paul left Titus on Crete to set in order what was unfinished, and the rest of the section shows what that means. The first half, verses 5 to 9, is a portrait of the leader the churches need. The second half, verses 10 to 16, is a portrait of the opposite, the teachers who must be stopped. The two halves are joined by a single hinge word, sound, which describes the elder's teaching in verse 9 and the believers' faith in verse 13. The healthy teacher produces healthy people, and the sick teacher spreads sickness.

The qualification list is built on a pattern of three. It begins with the one comprehensive demand, blameless, repeated at the start of verse 6 and again at the start of verse 7, as though everything else is an unpacking of it. Then come the home life in verse 6, the negatives in verse 7 (five things the overseer must not be), and the positives in verses 8 and 9 (six things he must be, climaxing in the demand to hold the faithful word). Character and doctrine are placed in one list because Paul will not let either stand without the other.

Verses 10 to 16 move from description to command: silence them, rebuke them sternly, pay no attention to their myths. The section closes with a cutting epigram in verse 16 that mirrors the very first words of the letter. Paul began by describing himself as a servant of God and apostle for the sake of the faith of God's elect, 1:1, and he ends the paragraph with people who claim to know God while their actions deny Him. The quoted Cretan proverb in verse 12 is the one place in the chapter where Paul borrows a voice that is not his own, and he does it to land a blow.
context.historical:
Crete is a long island south of the Aegean, and it had a Jewish presence long before Paul. Cretans are among those listed as hearing the gospel at Pentecost, Acts 2:11, and some of them may have carried it home. Paul's ship passed along its southern coast on the way to Rome, Acts 27:7-13. The letter assumes that churches already exist in many towns but have no settled leadership, which fits a mission that moved fast and left work behind. Titus is the delegate who finishes it.

The office he is to fill was familiar. Elders ruled Israel's towns, Deuteronomy 21:19, and Jewish synagogues were led by them. In the churches Paul planted, appointing elders was the regular follow up to evangelism, Acts 14:23. Elder and overseer are two names for one role: in Acts 20:17 Paul summons the elders of Ephesus and in verse 28 tells them that the Spirit made them overseers. The word elder stresses maturity and standing in the community; overseer stresses the work of watching over others.

The Cretan quotation comes from a poet and seer of the island, Epimenides, who lived centuries earlier, and the line about Cretans was proverbial in the Greek world. Paul quotes pagan poets elsewhere when they serve his argument, Acts 17:28 and 1 Corinthians 15:33. The false teachers are said to be especially those of the circumcision, verse 10, Jewish believers who pressed the law and Jewish traditions, verse 14, much like the circle Paul meets in Galatians 2:12. Because they taught for gain, verse 11, and went house to house, they were attacking the very unit in which these small churches met.
context.canonical:
This passage stands beside 1 Timothy 3:1-7 as one of the two main New Testament lists of qualifications for church leaders, and comparing them is instructive. The two lists overlap heavily on marriage, hospitality, self-control, gentleness and freedom from greed. Titus has no line about a recent convert, 1 Timothy 3:6, and spells out the leader's duty to refute opponents with more force, which suits a church on Crete that was just beginning. Paul never says the lists are exhaustive; they sketch a character that the whole letter goes on to describe for every believer.

The wider Bible has been preparing for this portrait. When Moses needed helpers, he was told to choose capable men who fear God, who are trustworthy and who hate dishonest gain, Exodus 18:21, a striking anticipation of verse 7. Ezekiel 34 condemns shepherds who feed themselves instead of the flock, and Jeremiah 23 promises shepherds after God's own heart. Peter addresses elders as fellow elder, telling them to shepherd willingly and not for shameful gain, 1 Peter 5:1-4. Hebrews 13:17 tells believers that their leaders watch over them as those who will give an account.

The warnings about false teachers link to Jesus' warning against wolves in sheep's clothing, known by their fruit, Matthew 7:15-20, to Paul's farewell to the Ephesian elders, Acts 20:29-30, and to the final letters of Paul and Peter, 2 Timothy 4:3-4 and 2 Peter 2:1-3. The line about those who profess to know God but deny Him by deeds is a short form of 2 Timothy 3:5, a form of godliness that denies its power.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
Paul is writing to equip a younger colleague for a task he cannot finish alone. The first thing he gives Titus is a list that tells him what to look for, and the order of the list matters. Almost nothing on it concerns gifts, charm or energy. It is about reputation in the home and the town, mastery of temper, money and appetite, and loyalty to the word as it was taught. Paul wants the churches to be led by people already living the gospel in the most ordinary places, since a leader's household shows what his leadership will look like.

The second thing he gives is permission to be firm. Titus is a gentle man of tested loyalty, but the false teachers are taking whole households apart for money, and a leader who will not name them is not leading. The weapons Paul offers are not force but the faithful word, used to encourage the sound and to refute the contradicting. The goal in verse 13 is that the deceived become sound in the faith. Paul also wants the first hearers, the Cretan believers who would hear this letter read aloud, to see their own island's reputation named, so that they would choose to be the exception.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The qualification list is prescriptive: it tells the church what kind of person to appoint. It is not a checklist of every possible virtue, and the same character is described in different words in 1 Timothy 3, which shows that Paul is painting a type rather than quoting a statute. The Cretan proverb is descriptive. Paul reports a proverb as true of the people he is dealing with and uses it for a purpose, which is why he immediately commands a stern rebuke aimed at health, verse 13. It does not hand anyone permission to stereotype a nation.

The command to silence the false teachers is addressed to Titus as a delegate with apostolic authority, in a particular church setting where the teachers were upsetting households. It supports firm, public correction of teaching that harms the church, but the tools are the ones Paul names: refuting by sound teaching, rebuking, and refusing to be drawn into myths. Today the section asks every church to test its leaders by character and doctrine together, and asks every believer to ask whether their own profession is matched by their deeds, verse 16.

debates.question: What does the phrase husband of but one wife require?

views.label: A one-woman man, faithful in marriage
views.case: The Greek literally reads 'a one-woman man.' Many read it as a demand for marital faithfulness and sexual integrity, whether or not the elder is currently married, since in the same verse Paul asks that his home life give no ground for accusation. The BSB footnote points this way. On this view the phrase says nothing about whether an unmarried or widowed man may serve.

views.label: No polygamy, and no remarriage after divorce
views.case: Others take it to exclude a man who has more than one wife, and some also a man who has remarried after divorce or after a wife's death, because the phrase seems to describe a single marital history. Supporters point to the care Paul takes with marriage and household order across the Pastorals.

views.label: Married with a stable household
views.case: A smaller group holds that elders were expected to be married men, since the next phrase assumes children and 1 Timothy 3:4-5 links ruling the church to ruling a household. Against this, Paul was himself unmarried, 1 Corinthians 7:7-8, and models devoted ministry.

debates.bearing: All three views fix on the same concern: an elder's marriage must be marked by fidelity that gives no ground for accusation. The wording is compact enough that churches have held different practices, so the surest conclusion is that the heart of the phrase is faithfulness.

debates.question: Does 'children who are believers' require every child to be a Christian?

views.label: Children who are believing, as the BSB reads
views.case: The word translated believers, pistos, can mean one who believes. On this reading Paul wants children who share the faith, a sign of a father's teaching and influence that gives credibility to his leadership in God's household.

views.label: Children who are faithful or trustworthy
views.case: The same word often means faithful or reliable, and it is paired with the charge of not being wild or insubordinate. Some take the line to mean children who are not known as rebels, whatever their stage of faith. Grown children, or young ones who have not yet made a profession, would not on this view disqualify the father.

debates.bearing: Paul's real test is the evidence of a household that is under order and not scandalous, since a man who cannot lead his home cannot be expected to lead God's church, 1 Timothy 3:5. Most churches apply it with pastoral wisdom, looking at the pattern of a man's family life, not at one child's lowest moment.

debates.question: Why would Paul quote a pagan Cretan prophet?

views.label: A true proverb used for rebuke
views.case: Paul says the testimony is true, verse 13, and calls for a stern rebuke. Pagan poets could speak truth about human nature, and Paul uses a line his readers knew well to show that the cultural vices have entered the church's teaching.

views.label: A rhetorical hook, not an ethnic verdict
views.case: Because Paul is writing to Cretan believers, and wants them sound in the faith, the line cannot be a verdict on every person. The same letter describes how Cretans, once enslaved to desires, can be washed and renewed, 3:3-5.

debates.bearing: Whichever emphasis one prefers, the pastoral purpose is the same: the proverb names a real temptation of the culture, and the churches are called to be the proof that the gospel changes people.

study.originalLanguages:
Several words in this passage carry more than the English suggests. The verb in verse 5 for set in order, epidiorthoo, is built on a root that means to straighten what is crooked or lacking, with a prefix meaning further. Paul pictures a work half done: the churches exist, but crooked things need straightening and gaps need filling. The related word for unfinished or lacking, from the root leipo, returns in 3:13, where Titus is told to make sure Zenas and Apollos lack nothing. Paul begins and ends the lesson on supply and completion.

The word blameless, anenkletos, opens both verse 6 and verse 7, though the BSB renders the second one above reproach. It means that no charge can be brought against a person, not that no fault exists. It is the word used of believers presented to God in 1 Corinthians 1:8 and Colossians 1:22, so it describes a reputation that holds when tested by neighbours. The word for insubordinate in verse 6, anupotaktos, describes the unruly, and appears again in verse 10 for the rebellious teachers, which ties the home and the false teachers together.

The word for self-willed in verse 7, authades, describes someone pleased with himself and hard to persuade, and Peter uses it of false teachers in 2 Peter 2:10. A leader who must hold to the faithful word cannot be a man who bends every word to himself.

Verse 9 gives two jobs for the one verb phrase. The overseer encourages, parakaleo, and refutes, elegcho, and the same verb for refute appears in verse 13 in the command to rebuke them sternly. The rarer word for sternly, apotomos, is related to the noun Paul uses of God's severity in Romans 11:22; it means cut off, with no softening. Titus is to be as firm in rebuke as the situation requires, but the goal, that they be sound, shows the love that drives it.

The word hold firmly in verse 9, antechomai, means to cling to something, and the thing clung to is the faithful word as it was taught, the apostolic message handed down. In verse 10 the false teachers are full of mataiologoi, empty talk, while the word of verse 11 for silencing, epistomizo, pictures putting a stopper in the mouth. Finally, in verse 16 the word for unfit, adokimos, means failed the test, the same word Paul uses of himself in 1 Corinthians 9:27 when he fears being disqualified. People who deny God by their deeds, using the verb arneomai, will be tested and found wanting.

typology.type: The elder as shepherd of God's flock, Titus 1:5-9
typology.fulfillment: Israel's elders and shepherds anticipated a leader who would care for God's people faithfully. Moses asked God for a man to lead the community so that it would not be like sheep without a shepherd, Numbers 27:16-17, and Ezekiel 34 promises that God Himself will come and shepherd His flock, followed by one shepherd, His servant David, Ezekiel 34:23. Jesus says He is the good shepherd who lays down His life for the sheep, John 10:11. Elders are the undershepherds of the Chief Shepherd, 1 Peter 5:4. The pattern falls short in that earthly elders are sinners who need the same grace they preach, while Christ never fails the flock.

typology.type: The household of God and its steward, verse 7
typology.fulfillment: The overseer is called God's steward, a manager of someone else's house. Joseph managed Potiphar's house and later Pharaoh's, Genesis 39:4 and 41:40, and faithful stewards in Jesus' parables are put in charge of the master's household, Luke 12:42-44. Hebrews sets Moses as faithful in God's house as a servant, and Christ as faithful over God's house as a son, Hebrews 3:5-6. The elder serves inside a house he did not build and does not own. The correspondence breaks where it must: Christ is the builder and owner of the house, the elder only a servant in it.

typology.type: False teachers and the false prophets of Israel
typology.fulfillment: The people who undermine whole households for gain recall the false prophets who spoke peace where there was no peace and prophesied for money, Jeremiah 6:13-14 and Micah 3:11. Moses had already told Israel to test any prophet by whether he led people away from the Lord, Deuteronomy 13:1-5. Jesus carries the pattern forward, warning of false prophets who come in sheep's clothing, Matthew 7:15, and the apostles describe the same figures in the church, 2 Peter 2:1-3. The pattern shows the test remains constant, doctrine and fruit together, but it also shows that the church is never promised an end to counterfeits before Christ returns.

typology.type: The pure and the defiled, verse 15
typology.fulfillment: Israel's law drew lines between clean and unclean, and the teachers on Crete were pressing such rules on Christians. Jesus taught that what goes into a person does not defile him but what comes out of the heart, Mark 7:14-23, and Paul says nothing is unclean in itself, Romans 14:14. The correspondence is that Christ fulfils the clean and unclean laws by cleansing the person from within, Acts 10:15, Hebrews 9:13-14. The old rules were a tutor; verse 15 shows that defilement of the mind and conscience, which no ritual can reach, is the real problem and only Christ's blood can answer it.

study.christ:
Christ is not named in verses 5 to 16, yet He stands behind every line. The first connection is that He is the Chief Shepherd for whom the elders work. Peter calls Him the Shepherd and Overseer of your souls, 1 Peter 2:25, using the same noun Paul uses here, episkopos, and so the word for the church's leaders is first of all His own title. The overseer is called God's steward, and the one who is faithful over God's house as a Son is Jesus, Hebrews 3:6. The qualities asked of elders, blameless, self-controlled, hospitable, gentle, holy, are an outline of His own character, and they are asked of elders because they have been seen perfectly in Him. He is the pattern before He is the standard.

The second connection is the faithful word. The elder must hold firmly to it as it was taught, verse 9, and that word is the message that begins in 1:1-3 with the hope of eternal life promised before the ages began and made known in the apostolic preaching. Jesus is the content of that message, and He is also called Faithful and True, Revelation 19:11. Holding to the faithful word is holding to Christ, since the apostolic teaching is not a theory but the testimony to a person.

Third, the sharp contrast of verse 16, people who claim to know God while their actions deny Him, shows what Christ is not. He is the Word made flesh, whose works and words agree, John 5:36 and 8:29, and who calls His followers to be known by their fruit. Those who deny Him by their works are the opposite of the Son who always did what pleased the Father.

Fourth, the pure and the defiled of verse 15 echoes Jesus' teaching that the heart is the source of defilement, Mark 7:20-23. His answer to the problem of a defiled mind and conscience is not a better set of rules but His own blood, which purifies the conscience, Hebrews 9:14. The Cretans needed more than correction; they needed someone to make them clean, and that person is introduced in chapters 2 and 3.

Guard against reading too much. This passage does not hide Christ in the list of qualifications. It shows what His body needs: leaders who resemble Him and teaching that points to Him. The elders do not stand between the church and Christ; they stand next to the church, pointing to the one who is Shepherd of them all.
study.god:
The most striking fact about God in this passage is how seriously He takes the people who serve in His house. He is not satisfied with a profession. Verse 16 says some claim to know Him while their actions deny Him, and the passage assumes God is not fooled. He is a God of truth, and the letter began by naming Him as the God who does not lie, 1:2. The Cretan reputation for lying forms the dark background. Against a culture proverbial for deceit, Paul sets a God whose word cannot fail and who therefore asks His servants to be truthful, upright and trustworthy.

He is also a God who orders His people. The phrase set in order, verse 5, shows that disorder is not His design and that the churches need structure and leadership under His word. He is a God of households, and the overseer is called His steward, which means everything the leader holds is on loan. The church is not the elder's property. It is a household with a Master who will ask for an account, as Hebrews 13:17 and 1 Peter 5:4 imply.

He is holy and cares about the heart. Verse 15 shows that purity is not a matter of what we touch or eat but of the mind and conscience, and God looks at both. His standards are not arbitrary. He wants leaders free of greed, violence and drunkenness because these destroy people He loves. There is also tenderness: His purpose in the rebuke of verse 13 is that the deceived will be sound, so even His sternest instructions aim at healing.

He is also a God who protects. The false teachers are silenced because they upset entire households, and the God who made families does not leave them undefended. He provides defenders in the form of elders trained in sound teaching. He equips them with the word and with the authority to refute.

For worship, this passage turns us toward gratitude and prayer. We thank God for faithful leaders, we pray for them, and we ask Him to keep us from becoming people whose profession is louder than our lives. It also invites self-examination: if our deeds were the only evidence, what would they say about the God we claim to know?

crossReferences.note: The companion list of qualifications for an overseer. The two lists agree on blameless character, a faithful marriage, a well ordered home, self-control, hospitality and freedom from greed, and they differ in small details because they address different churches. Reading them together shows Paul describing a type of person, not a rigid checklist.

Paul and Barnabas appoint elders in every church after prayer and fasting. This is the model Titus is now following on Crete, and it shows that appointing elders was a normal step in the early mission, not an exception, with prayer and care surrounding the choice.

Paul's farewell to the Ephesian elders calls them overseers, tells them to shepherd the church of God, and warns that savage wolves will come from outside and men from within will distort the truth. It shows elder and overseer as one office and gives the very danger Titus faces on Crete.

Peter exhorts elders to shepherd willingly, not for shameful gain and not as lords over those entrusted to them, promising a crown when the Chief Shepherd appears. It matches the qualities of Titus 1:7 on greed and self-will, and gives the motive: the elder works for Christ.

When Moses needs help judging the people, Jethro advises choosing capable men who fear God, who are trustworthy and who hate dishonest gain. The requirements anticipate verse 7 on greed and verse 9 on being faithful, and show that character has always been the first test of leaders.

Jesus warns about false prophets who look harmless and are known by their fruit. The teachers of Titus 1:10-16 fit exactly, and Paul's verdict in verse 16, that they are unfit for any good deed, applies Jesus' test to men whose deeds disagree with their words.

Paul describes people with a form of godliness who deny its power. It is a close parallel to Titus 1:16, where people profess to know God and deny Him by their actions. Both texts treat a mismatch between claim and conduct as the clearest mark of counterfeit religion.

Jesus declares that nothing outside a person defiles him but what comes out of him, since evil proceeds from the heart. This is the teaching Paul draws on in Titus 1:15, where defiled minds and consciences make everything unclean to the defiled, however pure the rules they keep.

Paul quotes pagan poets to the Athenians, using their own words to point to the true God. The same method appears in Titus 1:12, with a Cretan prophet's line, which shows that quoting a secular source can serve the gospel when the point is true and the purpose is clear.

Believers are told to obey their leaders and submit, because the leaders keep watch over souls as those who will give an account. It sets the two sides of the relationship: leaders answer to God for the flock, and the flock should make their work a joy by following sound leaders.

study.oneStory:
From the beginning God has chosen to care for His people through leaders He provides. In Eden He walked with Adam and Eve. After the fall, He raised up patriarchs, Moses, elders and judges, and then kings, and the sorry story of Israel's leaders, shepherds who fed themselves, runs through the prophets. Ezekiel 34 is the high point of that complaint and of the promise that follows. God will search for His sheep Himself, and He will set over them one shepherd, His servant David. The gospel announces that this has happened in Jesus, who is the good shepherd, and who rose from the dead and now rules His church, Hebrews 13:20.

Titus 1:5-16 belongs to the time between the Shepherd's first and second coming. He has gone up, and He has given His church the gifts of apostles, shepherds and teachers, Ephesians 4:11-12, so that the body is built up and no longer tossed about by every wind of teaching. The elders of Crete are part of that provision. Their work is to guard the faithful word and to protect the church from those who would turn God's house into a marketplace. It is humble, unglamorous work, and it keeps a people ready for His coming.

The warning in the second half of the passage is part of the same story. Since the serpent's question in Eden, 'Did God really say?', false teaching has threatened every generation of God's people. Israel's false prophets, Jesus' wolves and the Cretan teachers are different faces of one old attack on the word. God answers with sound teachers and with a people who are changed by the gospel, so that the world sees the difference.

The story ends with a flock that needs no further guarding. In Revelation 7:17 the Lamb in the midst of the throne becomes their shepherd and guides them to springs of living water. The elders of Crete and the stewards of every age will give their account and be glad to lay down their work. The false teachers and their myths will be gone, and the people who once were liars, beasts and gluttons will stand cleansed, with nothing left to deny the God they know.

sermon.title: Elders, Part One
sermon.why: Part of Begg's series A Study in Titus, this message expounds Titus 1:5-9, the charge to appoint elders and the character of the overseer, showing why the church needs leaders whose lives match the faithful word they hold. A careful, orthodox treatment of this movement's core.

quiz.q: Why did Paul leave Titus on Crete?

options.text: To set in order what was unfinished and appoint elders in every town.
options.note: This is Paul's stated reason in verse 5.

options.text: To collect money from the churches.
options.note: Paul in fact warns against leaders greedy for gain; his aim was godly order.

options.text: To start entirely new churches from scratch.
options.note: The churches existed already; Titus was to finish organising and lead them.

options.text: To take a rest from ministry.
options.note: Titus was left for demanding work, not rest.

quiz.q: What does Paul emphasise most in the qualifications for an elder?

options.text: Proven, blameless character and soundness in the faith.
options.note: The list is dominated by character and holding firmly to the word, verses 6-9.

options.text: Impressive speaking ability and popularity.
options.note: He must teach soundly, but the stress is on character, not charisma.

options.text: Wealth and social standing.
options.note: Paul warns against greed for money; status is not the point.

options.text: Formal education credentials.
options.note: The focus is godly character and grasp of the faithful word, not diplomas.

quiz.q: What are the two purposes of an elder holding firmly to the faithful word?

options.text: To encourage others by sound teaching and to refute those who contradict it.
options.note: Verse 9 names both the positive and the corrective task.

options.text: To win debates and build a personal following.
options.note: Refuting error is real, but the aim is the church's health, not a following.

options.text: To keep the teaching secret from outsiders.
options.note: The word is to be taught and defended openly, not hidden.

options.text: To replace Scripture with his own ideas.
options.note: He holds firmly to the word as taught, not his own inventions.

quiz.q: What was wrong with the false teachers on Crete?

options.text: They spread empty talk and deception for gain, wrecking households.
options.note: Verses 10-11 describe rebellious deceivers driven by dishonorable gain.

options.text: They simply used a different worship style.
options.note: The issue was false doctrine and corrupt motives, not style.

options.text: They were too strict about minor rules.
options.note: They pushed Jewish myths and human commands, but the root was rejecting the truth.

options.text: They preached the gospel too plainly.
options.note: They opposed the truth; their teaching was the problem.

quiz.q: How does Paul expose those who claim to know God but live ungodly lives?

options.text: They profess to know God, but by their actions they deny Him.
options.note: Verse 16 shows profession contradicted by conduct.

options.text: They know God fully and simply need more information.
options.note: Their problem is not lack of information but a defiled mind and denying works.

options.text: Their words matter and their actions do not.
options.note: Paul insists actions reveal the reality of a profession.

options.text: They are fully accepted despite their conduct.
options.note: Paul calls them unfit for any good deed; conduct exposes the claim.

questions: Paul chooses leaders by character before gifting. When you look for people to follow or to entrust with responsibility, how much weight do you give to proven character?
An elder is God's steward, managing what belongs to the Master. Where has God made you a steward of people, resources, or truth, and how faithfully are you handling it?
Self-control runs all through Titus. In which area of life is God calling you toward greater self-mastery right now?
The false teachers professed to know God but denied Him by their actions. Where might your daily conduct be sending a different message from your words about God?
Sound teaching is meant to keep us healthy in the faith. Who are the faithful voices you are letting shape you, and are you giving weight to teaching that is genuinely sound?

translationNotes.note: The husband of but one wife translates a phrase literally meaning a one-woman man; the BSB footnote offers faithful to his wife, stressing marital fidelity.
Elder in verse 5 and overseer here refer to the same office, viewed as mature standing and as watchful oversight.
The quotation Cretans are always liars is attributed to the Cretan poet-prophet Epimenides of Knossos, the so-called Epimenides paradox, as the BSB footnote notes.
